why: One mean per window of length k is a classic fixed-size sliding window: keep a running double sum, add the entering value and subtract the leaving one. The IEEE twist is that NaN and infinities poison a running sum, so keep counts of NaN, +Inf and -Inf in the window and sum only the finite values.
hints: If you add +Infinity to a running sum, can you ever subtract it back out? What about NaN?
No, so never put special values in the sum. Track three counters (NaN, +Inf, -Inf) for the window plus a double sum of finite values; the counters decide the result whenever any is non-zero.

Decode bits with struct, slide the window updating counters and sum in O(1), then emit: NaN if nanCount or both infinities, otherwise +/-Inf, otherwise float32(sum / k) bits with -0.0 mapped to +0.0. O(n).
pitfalls: Inputs are signed 32-bit ints; mask with 0xFFFFFFFF before decoding, and outputs must match the expected sign convention (negative infinity appears as -8388608).
Any NaN payload counts as NaN, but the output is always 0x7fc00000.
Converting a large double to float32 can overflow; map that to the matching infinity rather than crashing.
A zero mean must be returned as +0 bits even if the arithmetic yields -0.0.
